l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. X.
s: The army was terrified and disorganized by the lightning, thunder, and hail. Its soldiers dropped their arms, wandered through the woods in scattered groups, sought shelter and fires, and suffered many deaths from the cold.

l: the storm, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. X.
s: The storm developed over several days, culminating in continual lightning and thunder followed by a violent torrent of hail. It became as dark as night, overwhelmed the army, and was eventually somewhat abated.

l: hail, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. X.
s: The hail fell with such violence that the soldiers covered themselves with their shields and then dropped their arms when their hands became numb and frozen. The cold froze the hail as many soldiers lay or wandered in the woods.

l: the cold, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. X.
s: The cold overcame the soldiers' natural heat and left many immovable. It caused deaths among the army and camp attendants, although fires made from felled trees gradually revived some survivors.

l: the destruction of the army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. X.
s: The destruction caused by the storm and cold swept away a thousand soldiers and other mean attendants upon the camp. Some of the dead were reportedly found standing beside trees in the same postures they had held when they died.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Alexander fell in love with Roxana, the daughter of Oxyartes, and married her. Roxana was considered the most beautiful lady in Asia after Darius's wife, and Alexander refused to treat her dishonourably as a captive. Alexander also spared Darius's wife, showing continency and concern for his honour, and induced many friends to marry the daughters of leading barbarian men.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Alexander fell in love with Roxana upon seeing her and married her without treating her dishonourably as a captive. He also spared Darius's wife and induced many of his friends to marry the daughters of chief men among the barbarians.

l: Roxana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Roxana was the daughter of Oxyartes and a virgin of marriageable age. Alexander's fellow-soldiers judged her to be the most beautiful lady in Asia after Darius's wife, and Alexander married her.

l: Darius's wife, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Darius's wife was esteemed the most beautiful lady in all Asia. Alexander neither desired her unlawfully nor commanded her to his bed, instead sparing her out of reverence for her person and concern for his honour.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Asia is described as the region in which Roxana was considered the second most beautiful lady, after Darius's wife. Darius's wife was esteemed the most beautiful lady in all Asia.

l: marriage, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Alexander married Roxana and induced many of his friends to marry the daughters of chief men among the barbarians.

l: Alexander's falling in love with Roxana, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XI.
s: Alexander fell deeply in love with Roxana upon seeing her. He would not use her dishonourably as a captive and took her for his wife.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexander moved his army from Bactria toward India, leaving Amyntas with 3,500 horse and 10,000 foot in Bactria. He reorganized Alexandria in Paropamisus, appointed governors, received Taxiles and other princes, and divided his forces to advance toward the Indus. Hephsestion and Perdiccas besieged and captured the city of Astes after thirty days, while Alexander led another force through the territories of the Aspians, Phyrseans, and Arosacans. Alexander captured the first city he attacked after a brief assault, was slightly wounded, and ordered its prisoners put to the sword.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexander moved from Bactria toward India, reorganized Alexandria in Paropamisus, appointed governors, and directed his commanders to secure the country and prepare to cross the Indus. He led a rapid advance through the territories of the Aspians, Phyrseans, and Arosacans, captured the first city he attacked, and was slightly wounded by a dart.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: India was the region toward which Alexander and his army advanced after leaving Bactria.

l: Bactria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexander left Bactria with his army and left Amyntas there with 3,500 horse and 10,000 foot.

l: Alexander's army, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexander's army advanced from Bactria toward India and was divided near the river Cophas. Part of it went with Hephaestion and Perdiccas toward the Indus, while Alexander led the remaining forces through mountainous country.

l: Alexandria, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexandria, which Alexander had built in Paropamisus during his first expedition into Bactria, was repopulated with inhabitants from neighboring countries and Macedonians no longer fit for war. Alexander removed its governor for bad behavior, appointed Nicanor as governor, and appointed Tyriaspes over the wider region.

l: Taxiles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Taxiles came to Alexander with other petty princes, brought large presents, and promised to send twenty-five elephants. He accompanied Hephaestion and Perdiccas into Peucelaotis with other commanders and later helped Alexander trust Sangius, who had deserted Astes.

l: Peucelaotis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Peucelaotis was the country into which Hephaestion and Perdiccas were sent with troops to take the towns by force or persuasion and prepare for crossing the Indus.

l: Hephaestion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Hephaestion led forces with Perdiccas into Peucelaotis and besieged the city into which Astes had withdrawn. After thirty days he captured the city and Astes was killed.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: The Indus was the river toward which Hephaestion and Perdiccas were sent. They were ordered to prepare everything necessary to cross it, with Taxiles and other local commanders assisting.

l: Astes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Astes, the governor of Peucelaotis, attempted to revolt and withdrew into a city. Hephaestion besieged and captured it after thirty days, and Astes was killed.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: The Macedonians helped repopulate Alexandria with men no longer fit for war and formed the main force in Alexander's advance. They captured the outward and inner walls of the first city Alexander attacked, pursued fleeing inhabitants, and killed the prisoners.

l: first city attacked by Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: The first city attacked by Alexander resisted his initial advance but was driven back behind its walls. Its outer wall was taken the next day, its inner wall was then scaled, and the defenders fled toward the mountains; the city was subsequently leveled.

l: the siege of Astes's city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: The siege of Astes's city lasted thirty days and was conducted by Hephaestion. The city was captured, Astes was killed, and Sangius was made its governor.

l: Alexander's assault on the first city, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: Alexander's assault began when he defeated the defenders outside the first city and drove them inside. He was slightly wounded in the shoulder by a dart, then encamped against a suitable section of the wall; the Macedonians captured the outer wall the following morning and later scaled the inner wall.

l: massacre of the prisoners, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XII.
s: After the first city fell, the prisoners were put to the sword because Alexander had been wounded. Many inhabitants who fled toward the nearby mountains were also killed during the pursuit.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Alexander arrived at Nysa, whose inhabitants claimed that Bacchus had founded the city after conquering India. Acuphis, Nysa's chief man, asked Alexander to leave the city free in honor of Bacchus and described its foundation, laws, and surrounding landmarks. Alexander granted Nysa self-government, required three hundred horsemen, and accepted Acuphis's son and nephew instead of taking the city's leading men. He later visited Nysa and Mount Meros, sacrificed to Bacchus, and feasted with his friends.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Alexander arrived at Nysa and received Acuphis's request that he leave the city free in honor of Bacchus. He granted the Nysaeans liberty under their own laws, required three hundred horsemen, and appointed Acuphis governor of Nysaea. He later visited Nysa and Mount Meros, sacrificed to Bacchus, and feasted with his friends.

l: Bacchus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Bacchus was said to have conquered the Indians and founded Nysa as a memorial of his expedition. The Nysaeans asked Alexander to spare their city out of reverence for Bacchus, and Alexander sacrificed to him after visiting Mount Meros.

l: Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Nysa was presented as a city founded by Bacchus for soldiers who were unfit for war and descended from his family. It governed itself under an aristocracy until Alexander granted it continued freedom, and it was said to be the only place in India where ivy grew.

l: Acuphis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Acuphis, the chief man of Nysa, led the delegation that asked Alexander to preserve the city's freedom. He persuaded Alexander not to take a hundred of Nysa's leading men and was appointed governor of Nysaea; his son and his nephew were sent to Alexander.

l: India, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: India was the region through which Alexander passed between the Cophen and Indus rivers. The text says that Bacchus had conquered the Indians, while ivy was otherwise absent from India.

l: Nysaea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Nysaea was the country associated with Nysa. Alexander made Acuphis governor of the whole province of Nysaea.

l: Meros, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Meros was the mountain overlooking Nysa. It was said to have received its name, meaning a thigh, because Bacchus was fabled to have been cherished in his father's thigh; Alexander later visited it to see its ivy, laurel, and shady groves.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: The Macedonians were expected by Alexander to emulate the deeds of Bacchus and willingly endure further toils. They especially enjoyed seeing the ivy at Nysa because they had not seen any for a long time.

l: Nysaeans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: The Nysaeans sent Acuphis and thirty other leading men to ask Alexander to leave their city free. Alexander granted their request and allowed them to continue governing themselves according to their own laws.

l: the aristocracy of Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: The aristocracy of Nysa consisted of three hundred men and governed the city. Alexander initially demanded one hundred of them, but after Acuphis's argument he abandoned that demand.

l: Nysa's laws, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Nysa's laws allowed the city to be governed under an aristocracy. Alexander learned of this constitution, commended it, and allowed the Nysaeans to continue governing according to their own laws.

l: Dionysius's Indian expedition, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Dionysius's Indian expedition was described as a conquest of the Indians followed by a return toward the Grecian sea. The expedition was said to have led to the foundation of Nysa as a memorial of his victory.

l: Alexander's arrival at Nysa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: When Alexander arrived at Nysa, Acuphis and thirty other leading men approached him as ambassadors. They asked him to leave the city free in honor of Bacchus, and Alexander accepted their request.

l: Nysa's foundation, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Nysa's foundation was attributed to Bacchus, who supposedly built it for soldiers of his family who were unserviceable for war. The city was said to have been named after Bacchus's nurse, while the surrounding country was called Nysaea.

l: ivy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIII.
s: Ivy was said to grow nowhere in India except at Nysa, which the Nysaeans offered as evidence that Bacchus had founded the city. Alexander and the Macedonians viewed the ivy on Mount Meros, and some of it was used to crown their heads while they sang praises to Bacchus.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: Alexander marched against Massaga, the greatest city of the country, after the barbarians dispersed into separate cities. The city was defended by seven thousand mercenary Indians, who fought fiercely against the Macedonians during a four-day siege. After the governor was killed and many defenders were lost or wounded, the mercenary Indians agreed to join Alexander but camped separately and planned to flee. Alexander surrounded their hill at night and put them all to the sword, then stormed and captured Massaga.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: Alexander led the Macedonians against Massaga and directed the battle, the assaults, and the siege works. He agreed to spare the mercenary Indians if they joined his army, but when they planned to flee, he surrounded their hill at night and put them all to the sword. He then took Massaga by storm.

l: Massaga, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: Massaga was the greatest city of the country and was defended by mercenary Indians. After the defenders were killed or withdrawn, Alexander captured the city by storm and took the mother and daughter of Assacenus.

l: barbarians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: The barbarians dispersed into several cities rather than face Alexander's army in a body. At Massaga, they joined the mercenary Indians in resisting the Macedonians and were driven back into the city after a fierce engagement.

l: Macedonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: The Macedonians fought the defenders of Massaga, initially drawing them away from the city before turning upon them. They endured several difficult assaults, including the collapse of a bridge from a wooden tower, and ultimately captured the city.

l: mercenary Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: Seven thousand mercenary Indians entered Massaga to assist its defenders and fought fiercely against Alexander's army. After the governor was killed and many of their men were lost or wounded, they agreed to join Alexander, but planned to flee rather than fight other Indians. Alexander surrounded them at night and killed every one of them.

l: Massaga siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: The siege lasted four days. The Macedonians used engines, a wooden tower, bridges, archers, and repeated assaults, but the defenders held until their governor was killed and many men became unserviceable. Alexander then captured Massaga by storm after executing the mercenary Indians.

l: execution of the mercenary Indians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, SUP. XIV.
s: After the mercenary Indians agreed to join Alexander but camped separately and prepared to flee during the night, Alexander surrounded their hill with his forces. He put every one of them to the sword.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Books XIV–XVI recount wars, revolutions, tyrannies, and shifting alliances among the Greek cities, Persia, Sicily, and Italy. They describe the rule of the Thirty at Athens, the rise and actions of Dionysius I, the Persian expeditions involving Cyrus and Artaxerxes, and the wars of the Lacedaemonians, Thebans, Athenians, and others. The narrative includes the campaigns of Agesilaus, Epaminondas, Pelopidas, Timoleon, and Philip, as well as the Social War, the Phocian War, and the Battle of Chaeronea. It ends with Philip's preparations for war against Persia and his murder, while also recounting the careers and deaths of Dionysius the Younger, Dion, and Timoleon.

l: Athenians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Athenians disagreed about the form of their government, and the Thirty were established at Athens. They fought in the Social War, aided Byzantium against Philip, opposed Philip's expansion, and were defeated at Chaeronea.

l: Lacedaemonians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Lacedaemonians concluded peace with the Athenians and established oligarchies in many cities. They fought Mantinea, the Olynthians, the Thebans, and the confederates opposing them, and were routed at Leuctra and later at Mantinea.

l: Athens, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Athens was governed by the Thirty, whose rule was marked by cruelty, especially toward Theramenes. The Athenians later seized Acte and resisted Philip's growing power.

l: Dionysius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Dionysius strengthened his sovereignty in Sicily, dispersed the Syracusans, fortified Epipolae, and fought the Rhegines and Carthaginians. He captured Motya, besieged Syracuse and Rhegium, conquered or destroyed several Italian cities, and died after a later war against the Carthaginians.

l: Syracusans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Syracusans revolted against Dionysius but were dispersed. Syracuse was later besieged, and the Syracusans resisted Dionysius under the leadership of Theodorus and others.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Syracuse was besieged during the war between Dionysius and the Carthaginians. It later became the place to which the inhabitants of Catonia were transplanted and was contested during the struggles involving Dionysius the Younger, Dion, and Hicetas.

l: Byzantium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Byzantium was ruled tyrannically by Clearchus. It was later besieged by Philip, but the Athenians aided it and Philip raised the siege.

l: Thebans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Thebans subdued the Oropians, retook the Cadmea, and defeated the Spartans at Orchomenus and Leuctra. They later disagreed with the general peace, destroyed Plataea and Orchomenus, and joined the Athenians against Philip.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Thebes was the place where Philip had been held as a hostage. The Lacedaemonians seized the Cadmea at Thebes, but it was later retaken by the Thebans.

l: Cyrus the Younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Cyrus fought his brother Artaxerxes for the Persian throne. He was routed, and the Greek forces that had served him made a long and difficult march out of Persia.

l: Artaxerxes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Artaxerxes fought Cyrus for the Persian throne and later sought repeatedly to establish peace among the Greeks. He conducted expeditions against Evagoras and Egypt and died after the Egyptian and Greek conflicts described in the text.

l: Persia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Persia fought Cyrus, the Lacedaemonians, Evagoras, Egypt, and the Phocians' allies. Persian forces were defeated at Sipylos and in other engagements, though Persia later imposed or mediated peace among the Greeks.

l: Thrasybulus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Thrasybulus opposed the Thirty Tyrants at Athens. He is also mentioned as an Athenian general whose actions are recounted later in Book XIV.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Egypt was involved in the Persian wars and in conflicts over its kingship. Psammetichus cruelly treated his former friend Tamos, while Tachos fought Persia and later lost his kingdom before Agesilaus restored him.

l: Conon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Conon was made admiral of the Persian fleet. He commanded it in the sea-fight at Cnidus, where Pisander and the Lacedaemonian fleet were defeated.

l: Rhegium, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Rhegium was nearly surprised and later besieged by Dionysius. It eventually surrendered, and Philo, its governor, and his son were treated cruelly.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Carthaginians fought Dionysius repeatedly in Sicily. Their armies suffered a plague, their fleet was greatly destroyed in Syracuse's harbor, and they later made peace before renewing the war and eventually being defeated by Timoleon.

l: Agesilaus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Agesilaus was appointed by the Lacedaemonians to command the war against Persia. He routed the Persians at Sipylos and later defeated Egyptian forces that pursued him, restoring Tachos to his kingdom.

l: Corinth, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Corinth took part in the war against the Lacedaemonians and experienced a great sedition. Epaminondas later assaulted Corinth during his invasion of the Peloponnesus.

l: Romans, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Romans took Veii and dedicated a golden cup to Apollo. They were defeated by the Gauls at the Allia, saw Rome captured, and were later relieved when Marcus Furius routed the Gauls.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Rhodes revolted from the Athenians. It was later brought over to the Thebans by Epaminondas.

l: Evagoras, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Evagoras became king of Salamis in Cyprus and made war against Persia. Peace was eventually concluded with him, but he was later murdered in Cyprus by an eunuch.

l: Mantinea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Mantinea was besieged by the Lacedaemonians. It later became the site of the battle in which Epaminondas was killed, although the Lacedaemonians were routed.

l: Cadmea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Lacedaemonians seized the Cadmea at Thebes. The Cadmea was later retaken by the Thebans.

l: Pelopidas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Pelopidas was sent against the Olynthians and later led forces in the Peloponnesus. Alexander of Pherae imprisoned him and Ismenias, but Pelopidas was freed and later killed in the war against Alexander; the text praises him.

l: Leuctra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Leuctra was the site of a famous battle in which Epaminondas and the Thebans defeated the Spartans.

l: Alexander of Pherae, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Alexander of Pherae imprisoned Pelopidas and Ismenias and acted cruelly at Scotussa. He was later murdered by his wife and two brothers.

l: Epaminondas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Epaminondas led the Thebans at Leuctra and in invasions of the Peloponnesus, including an assault on Corinth. He brought Rhodes, Chios, and Byzantium over to the Thebans and was killed at Mantinea; the text commends him.

l: Gauls, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Gauls invaded Italy, defeated the Romans at the Allia, and captured Rome while the Romans were besieged in the Capitol. They were later routed by Marcus Furius and cut off in the plains of Trausium.

l: Sparta, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Sparta was besieged during Epaminondas's invasion of the Peloponnesus. Dionysius sent Gauls and Spaniards to assist the Lacedaemonians defending it.

l: Philip II of Macedon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Philip escaped from hostagehood at Thebes, defeated the Athenians, subdued the Paeonians, and routed the Illyrians. He took Amphipolis, Olynthus, Elatea, and other cities, raised the siege of Byzantium after Athenian intervention, defeated the Athenians at Chaeronea, and was made general of Greece before being murdered.

l: Dionysius the younger, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Dionysius the Younger acted in Sicily and other regions during the conflicts involving Dion and Syracuse. He was expelled by Timoleon.

l: Dion, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Dion fled to Corinth and later returned to Sicily. He entered Syracuse, defeated Dionysius's forces, and eventually left the Syracusans amid their troubled condition.

l: Social War, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Social War was fought between the Athenians and other allied states. Iphicrates and Timotheus were joined as admirals with Chares, and the war ended after Chares's actions against the Persians.

l: Phocian war, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Phocian War began when Philomelus seized the temple at Delphi after defeating the Locrians. Philomelus died in battle, Onomarchus succeeded him, and the war ended after Philip's intervention and the punishment of the Phocians.

l: Philomelus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Philomelus seized the temple at Delphi after defeating the Locrians and began the Phocian War. He was later killed in battle.

l: Timoleon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Timoleon went to Sicily, defeated Hicetas, and gained Syracuse. He expelled Dionysius, made good laws, defeated the Carthaginians in a remarkable victory, and died after his actions in Sicily.

l: Hicetas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Hicetas gained control of Syracuse during the struggles involving Dionysius and Dion. He was defeated by Timoleon, who then gained Syracuse.

l: Elatea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Elatea was taken by Philip. Its capture caused great consternation in Athens because of fear of Philip.

l: Chaeronea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Chaeronea was taken by Philip during his expansion in Greece.

l: Demosthenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: Demosthenes solicited the Boeotians to join the Athenians against Philip.

l: Battle of Chaeronea, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Battle of Chaeronea was fought between Philip and the Athenians. Philip won, and Lycurgus, the Athenian general, was put to death.

l: battle of Leuctra, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Battle of Leuctra was a famous victory of Epaminondas and the Thebans over the Spartans.

l: Sicilian wars, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XIV.
s: The Sicilian wars included Dionysius's struggles against the Syracusans, Rhegium, and the Carthaginians, as well as the later conflicts involving Dionysius the Younger, Dion, Hicetas, and Timoleon. Timoleon ultimately defeated the Carthaginians and restored order in Sicily.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Book XVII concerns Alexander’s campaigns from Macedonia through Asia, Egypt, Persia, India, and Gedrosia, including the destruction of Thebes, the capture of Tyre and Persepolis, the battles of Issus and Arbela, and Alexander’s death at Babylon. Book XVIII describes the succession crisis after Alexander, the division of the provinces, the revolt of the Greeks, the Lamian War, and conflicts among Perdiccas, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Eumenes, and other commanders. Book XIX follows Antigonus’s struggle against Eumenes and the other successors, Cassander’s actions in Macedonia and Greece, Seleucus’s recovery of Babylon, and Demetrius’s campaigns.

l: Book XVII, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It covers Alexander’s rise, conquests, battles, dealings with Darius, march through Asia and India, return through Gedrosia, and death at Babylon.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He became commander of the Amphictyons, invaded the Illyrians and others, destroyed Thebes, and invaded Asia. He defeated the Persians at Issus and Arbela, captured Tyre, Gaza, Persepolis, and many other places, marched as far as the Indus, and died at Babylon.

l: Thebes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It was besieged and destroyed by Alexander. Its sufferings are described, and later Cassander rebuilt Thebes.

l: Asia, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Alexander landed his army in Asia and conducted extensive campaigns there. The region was later divided among the chief commanders after Alexander’s death.

l: Persians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: They fought Alexander at the Granicus, Issus, and Arbela and were defeated. Alexander later mixed twenty thousand Persian archers with his army.

l: Darius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He prepared armies against Alexander, was defeated at Issus, and lost his mother, wife, two daughters, and son. He sent letters and offers to Alexander and was later murdered.

l: battle at Issus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It was a memorable battle in which Alexander defeated Darius. Darius’s mother, wife, two daughters, and son were captured, and Alexander treated them nobly.

l: Tyre, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It was besieged and taken by Alexander. The Tyrians used various inventions to defend themselves, and later Tyre was besieged and taken again during the wars among Alexander’s successors.

l: Greeks, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: They sent ambassadors to Alexander after the destruction of Thebes and later served as allies and auxiliaries in his campaigns. After Alexander’s death, the Greeks revolted, were defeated in the Lamian War, and eventually submitted, except for the Ætolians.

l: Arbela, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It was the site of the famous battle where the Persians were routed by Alexander.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It was affected by the revolt of the Greeks and the Lamian War. After Alexander’s death, its cities were contested by Antipater, Cassander, Antigonus’s commanders, and others.

l: Antipater, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He marched against Memnon in Thrace and defeated the Lacedæmonians, whose king Agis was killed. He helped defeat the revolting Greeks, became involved in the succession struggles, and was succeeded in Macedonia by Polyperchon.

l: Babylon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Alexander entered Babylon after the Chaldean astrologers had warned him against doing so, and he died there. In Book XIX, Antigonus’s army was entertained there by Seleucus, who later recovered the city with a small army.

l: Persepolis, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Alexander took Persepolis and gave it to his soldiers to plunder. Its citadel contained great riches, and the city was burned at the instigation of Phais.

l: Bessus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He stirred up the Bactrians after Darius’s death. He was brought before Alexander and punished.

l: Indus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Alexander marched to the Indus and later faced danger from whirlpools in the river. He reached the main ocean after campaigns in the surrounding regions.

l: Book XVIII, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It concerns the succession after Alexander’s death, the appointment of Arrhidaeus, and the division of the provinces. It describes the revolt of the Greeks, the Lamian War, Perdiccas’s invasion of Egypt, the struggles of Antigonus and Eumenes, and Cassander’s rise in Macedonia and Greece.

l: king Philip, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He was made king after Alexander’s death. The provinces were divided among the chief commanders, and he later joined the other kings under Eumenes.

l: Perdiccas, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He executed Meleager, affected the kingdom of Macedonia, and opposed Antigonus. He marched against Ptolemy in Egypt, suffered heavy losses at the Nile, and was killed.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He gained Egypt and allied with Antipater. He defeated or opposed several rivals, gained Syria and Phoenicia through Nicanor, and later joined Cassander, Seleucus, and Lysimachus against Antigonus.

l: Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He opposed Perdiccas, defeated Eumenes and Alcetas, and sought to become sovereign over all. He later fought Ptolemy, Seleucus, Cassander, and Lysimachus, while sending Demetrius against opposing forces.

l: Eumenes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He defeated Neoptolemus and Craterus, opposed Antigonus, and took refuge at Nora after being routed. He later continued the struggle in Asia but was eventually betrayed and killed.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He conspired against Polyperchon and became a leading power in Macedonia and Greece. He took the Piraeus, killed Nicanor, defeated or opposed Polyperchon’s allies, murdered Roxana and her son, and rebuilt Thebes.

l: Seleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He quarreled with Antigonus and fled to Ptolemy, who received him favorably. He later recovered Babylon with a small army and joined Ptolemy, Cassander, and Lysimachus against Antigonus.

l: Book XIX, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: It follows Antigonus’s campaigns against Eumenes and his rivals, the consolidation of Cassander’s power, and the activities of Ptolemy, Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Demetrius. It also describes conflicts in Macedonia, Greece, Asia, Sicily, and Italy.

l: Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: He entered Thrace and was defeated while attempting to relieve Antipater. He later joined Ptolemy, Cassander, and Seleucus against Antigonus and made peace with him.

l: Demetrius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XVII.
s: Antigonus left him in Syria to watch Ptolemy. He defeated Ptolemy’s general at Gaza, took Tyre, and was later sent against Seleucus in Babylon.

l: The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Agathocles invades Africa from Syracuse, burns his ships, defeats Carthaginian forces, and conducts further wars in Africa and Sicily, marked by repeated cruelty and eventual mutiny. Cassander and Polyperchon maneuver over the succession after Alexander, while Ptolemy, Antigonus, Demetrius, Lysimachus, and Seleucus engage in wars and shifting alliances across Egypt, Cyprus, Greece, and Asia. Demetrius besieges Rhodes, but peace is later made with the Rhodians. Affairs also continue in Italy, the Cimmerian Bosporus, and other regions, while Agathocles and his forces suffer reverses before making peace with the Carthaginians.

l: Agathocles, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Agathocles invades Africa, burns his ships, defeats Hanno and Bomilcar, and carries on campaigns in Africa and Sicily. He decoys and kills Ophelas, defeats Dinocrates's army, massacres seven thousand who submit on terms, and displays further cruelty at Aegesta and Syracuse. His army suffers reverses in Africa; his own men put him in chains, he escapes to Africa, and his two sons are killed before peace is made with the Carthaginians.

l: Africa, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Africa is invaded by Agathocles, who burns his ships and initially succeeds against the Carthaginians. His army is later blocked, nearly starved, defeated, and involved in a mutiny before peace is made with the Carthaginians.

l: Syracuse, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Syracuse is the base of Agathocles's actions and receives the spoils he sends from Cyrene. The Syracusans capture and execute Hanno, send his head to Agathocles, defeat and execute Hamilcar, and later suffer Agathocles's cruelty.

l: Carthaginians, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: The Carthaginians appoint Hanno and Bomilcar as generals against Agathocles, draw thirty thousand men from Carthage, and fight him in Africa and near Syracuse. They are described as practicing the sacrifice of their children, and they eventually make peace with Agathocles's soldiers.

l: Cassander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Cassander acts in Macedonia and instigates Polyperchon to murder Hercules, the son of Alexander. He later sends to Antigonus to make peace, joins with Lysimachus, Ptolemy, and Seleucus against Antigonus, and makes peace with Demetrius.

l: Polyperchon, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Polyperchon attempts to restore Hercules, the son of Alexander, but murders him at Cassander's instigation.

l: Alexander, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Alexander is referenced through his son Hercules, whom Polyperchon murders at Cassander's instigation, and through his sister Cleopatra, who is killed by the governor of Sardis.

l: Ptolemy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Ptolemy acts in Cilicia and elsewhere, comes to Corinth, and later goes to Cyprus. He fights Demetrius at sea and is routed, joins Cassander, Lysimachus, and Seleucus against Antigonus, and besieges Sidon before returning to Egypt on a false report.

l: Archagathus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Archagathus, the son of Agathocles, kills Lyciscus and is placed in great danger by the army. He also carries out actions in Africa.

l: Italy, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: The unit records continuing affairs and transactions in Italy, including the works of Appius Claudius and developments associated with Tarentines, Lucanians, and Cleonymus.

l: Demetrius, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Demetrius defeats the Greeks, takes the Piraeus, and acts in Cyprus and Greece. He fights Ptolemy at sea, besieges Rhodes, later leaves Greece for Asia, and makes peace with Cassander.

l: Greece, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Demetrius defeats the Greeks and conducts further actions there. Cassander and Demetrius assemble armies in Greece before Demetrius leaves after peace is made with Cassander.

l: Antigonus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Antigonus takes the title of king and marches against Egypt, losing some ships in a tempest near Raphia before returning to Syria. He refuses Cassander's offer of peace and is opposed by Lysimachus, Ptolemy, and Seleucus.

l: Sicily, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Sicily is the scene of actions by Agathocles, his captains, Dinocrates, and others. Agathocles's captains defeat Xenodochus, while Agathocles later defeats Dinocrates's large army there.

l: Dinocrates, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Dinocrates prevails in Sicily while Agathocles is willing to resign his government, but he does not accept the arrangement. Agathocles later routs his great army with few men, then takes Dinocrates into favor, and Dinocrates betrays the confederates.

l: Rhodes, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Rhodes is besieged by Demetrius, while its sea-captains conduct defensive actions. Peace is eventually made with the Rhodians.

l: Lysimachus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Lysimachus joins Cassander, Ptolemy, and Seleucus against Antigonus. Antigonus marches against him.

l: Seleucus, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Seleucus joins Cassander, Lysimachus, and Ptolemy against Antigonus. He later marches from Babylon with a great army.

l: Egypt, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: Antigonus marches into Egypt but loses ships in a tempest near Raphia and returns to Syria. Ptolemy returns to Egypt after abandoning the siege of Sidon because of a false report.

l: Rhodes siege, The Historical Library of Diodorus the Sicilian, BOOK XX.
s: The siege of Rhodes by Demetrius continues before peace is made with the Rhodians. The unit also records the actions of the Rhodian sea-captains during the siege.

l: The Argonautica
s: The Argonautica follows Jason’s quest for the golden fleece and the long, dangerous return of the Argonauts. Pelias, fearing an oracle that a one-sandaled man will cause his death, sends Jason to seek the fleece from Aeetes. With Athena’s help Argo is built, and heroes including Heracles, Orpheus, Polydeuces, and others join Jason. They elect Jason leader, sacrifice to Apollo, and sail from Iolcos. Their outward voyage brings both welcome and loss. On Lemnos they are received by Hypsipyle and the women who killed their husbands; Heracles eventually forces the companions to leave. A mistaken night battle with the Doliones kills their king Cyzicus, while Hylas is taken by a water-nymph and Heracles is left behind searching for him. Polydeuces kills the boxer-king Amycus, and the blind Phineus, freed from the Harpies by Zetes and Calais, gives the heroes crucial directions. Athena helps Argo pass the Cyanean rocks. Idmon and the helmsman Tiphys die before the company reaches the island of Ares, meets the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus, and arrives in Colchis. In Aea, Aeetes demands that Jason yoke fire-breathing bulls, plough Ares’ field, sow dragon’s teeth, and defeat the armed Earthborn men. Hera and Athena enlist Cypris and Eros so that Medea, Aeetes’ daughter, loves Jason. Torn between family and desire, Medea gives him a powerful charm and instructions; Jason completes the trials by making the Earthborn kill one another. When Aeetes plans resistance, Medea flees with Jason. She puts the guardian serpent to sleep, and Jason takes the fleece. The return is marked by pursuit, guilt, divine aid, and wandering. Medea lures her pursuing brother Apsyrtus into Jason’s trap, and Jason kills him; Zeus therefore requires their purification by Circe and imposes further hardships. Hera, Thetis, and the Nereids aid Argo through storms, the Wandering rocks, the Sirens, Scylla, and Charybdis. At Drepane, Alcinous allows Medea to remain with Jason after their marriage. Blown into Libya, the heroes carry Argo across the desert, lose Canthus and Mopsus, and regain the sea through Triton’s guidance. Medea defeats Talos in Crete; after further divine help and stops at Anaphe and Aegina, Jason and the surviving Argonauts finally return safely to Pagasae.

l: Phoebus, The Argonautica
s: Phoebus, Apollo called the Gleamer, hears Jason’s plea during the Pall of Darkness, descends to the Melantian rocks, and with his golden bow reveals Anaphe to bewildered men. He commands Boeotians and Nisaeans to worship Idmon as their city’s guardian.

l: Jason, The Argonautica
s: Jason is Aeson and Alcimede’s son, Cretheus’s grandson, and a hero who becomes leader of the Argonauts and commander of Argo. After crossing the Anaurus and losing a sandal, he comes before Pelias, whose response to an oracle sends him on the dangerous quest for the Golden Fleece. Guided by Apollo’s oracle, favored by Hera for carrying her when she appeared as an old crone, and comforted by Athena, he gathers the heroes, accepts their election as leader, sacrifices to Apollo, and departs from Pagasae. On the voyage Jason declines Hypsipyle’s sovereignty, manages conflicts and losses among the Argonauts, including the departure of Heracles, and leads dealings with Phineus, the sons of Phrixus, and others. He experiences fear for his comrades and their return to Hellas, but repeatedly regains resolve. At the Phasis he approaches Aeetes for the fleece; Aeetes imposes the contest of the bronze-footed, fire-breathing bulls, the serpent’s teeth, and the Earthborn men. As a stranger in Colchis, Jason receives Medea’s magical help. He promises her honor, remembrance, and marriage in Hellas, receives her dread charm, sacrifices to Hecate Brimo, and uses the charm to withstand and yoke the bulls, plough with the adamant plough, sow the teeth, and destroy the Earthborn men by turning them against one another. He then receives Medea, carries off the Golden Fleece, orders the return, and defends the ship from pursuit. During the return Jason and Medea deceive Apsyrtus, whom Jason ambushes and kills. He undergoes Circe’s purification for the killing, remains bound to Medea by oaths, and marries her in Macris’s sacred cave. He continues leading the Argonauts through sea and desert dangers, follows the counsel of Libyan nymphs, assists Medea against Talos, and calls on Phoebus during the Pall of Darkness. His course runs from Pelias’s command, through the fleece’s capture, to a perilous return shaped by leadership, divine aid, Medea’s help, and the consequences of Apsyrtus’s death.

l: Pelias, The Argonautica
s: Pelias is king of Iolcos who receives an oracle that a one-sandaled man will cause his death. When Jason arrives wearing one sandal, Pelias, fearing the prophecy, devises a dangerous voyage to remove him. He commands Jason and a great company of heroes on the expedition to seek the Golden Fleece from Aeetes, becoming Jason’s enemy through this demand. Pelias also neglects Pelasgian Hera at a banquet, leaving her without sacrifice and committing an outrage. Though Hera says he has escaped an evil doom, she intends that he repay this offense.

l: Argo, The Argonautica
s: Argo is a swift, excellent, well-benched ship: the heroes’ vessel, rowed and sailed by the Minyae and carrying Jason, his comrades, and the Argonauts in pursuit of the golden fleece. Athena fashions and guides its construction, with Argus helping by her counsels; it is the finest ship tested with oars, stronger than the ships of the Colchians, firm in its bolts, and able to endure blasts. A divine beam is fitted into the middle of its stem. Tiphys son of Hagnias commands and guides it at the helm. Prepared at Pagasae, Argo is dragged over rollers, launched, and furnished with oars, mast, sails, stores, anchors, ropes, and the divine beam. It first sails along the coast to Lemnos, then continues through the Hellespont, reaches Fair Haven and Chytus, is driven back to the Doliones, and waits through a twelve-day storm before departing again. It leaves the Mysian coast without Heracles and Hylas, passes the Bebrycians, and survives the Bosporus storm and great wave. Warned about the Cyanean rocks, it passes between them when Athena pushes it through; its stern-ornament is damaged, but the ship escapes. Argo proceeds past rivers, headlands, islands, and peoples to the island of Ares, then reaches the river Phasis. It carries dragon’s teeth after Aeetes gives them for the contest, receives Jason and his comrades after their tasks, and later carries Medea during the flight from Colchis. With the golden fleece aboard, it flees through Ister, the Cronian sea, and surrounding islands. The Nereids lift and guide it through the Wandering rocks, and it reaches Drepane, where Alcinous and the Phaeacians receive it. Its hardest later passage comes when it is thrust onto the shore of Syrtis. The heroes carry it across the Libyan desert for twelve days and nights, set it in the Tritonian lake, and Triton guides it back into the sea. It then sails past Carpathus to Crete, continues by Anaphe and Aegina, and returns at last to Pagasae.

l: golden fleece, The Argonautica
s: The golden fleece is a golden, immense fleece from the sacrificed golden ram, hanging on an oak in the sacred grove of Ares in the land of Aeetes. It is the central object and prize of Jason’s voyage with the assembled heroes: the expedition travels to Aeetes’s land seeking to take it and return with it. Though possessed by Aeetes, it is guarded by a sleepless dragon or serpent, and Aeetes believes that those seeking it aim to seize his power. He promises it to Jason only if Jason completes the required contest. Hera and Athena arrange for Medea’s love and assistance, and Medea tells Jason that he will carry the fleece away after the contest. In the end, Medea puts the guardian serpent to sleep, allowing Jason to take the fleece from the huge oak. Its brightness is like the rising sun, and aboard the ship Jason covers it with a newly woven mantle. The heroes retain it under a covenant even if it was won by craft rather than openly. Finally, it is spread over the bridal couch in Macris’s sacred cave to honor Jason and Medea’s marriage; its golden tufts shine like flame and inspire longing and awe among the nymphs.

l: Pontus, The Argonautica
s: Pontus is a sea entered after the Cyanean rocks; Phineus directs the Argonauts along its shores toward the Colchians and Aea.

l: Cyanean rocks, The Argonautica
s: The Cyanean rocks are twin, clashing rocks at the entrance to Pontus, where two seas meet and make passage perilous. Phineus tells the Argonauts to send a dove first. The dove escapes damaged; Athena drives Argo through as the rocks nearly destroy it. After a living man passes between them, the rocks become fixed together forever.

l: Poseidon, The Argonautica
s: A deity honoured by Pelias, father of Triton, whose car Amphitrite looses; Triton later guides Argo from the Tritonian lake into the sea.

l: Hera, The Argonautica
s: Hera is a goddess, chief among goddesses, wife and spouse of Zeus, and queen of marriage. She is an active divine protector and planner whose favor centers on Jason, Aeson’s son, because he once showed her pity while she was disguised as an old woman; she also seeks punishment for Pelias’s insult. She first nurtures the Earthborn as a trial for Heracles, then strengthens Ancaeus after the deaths of Idmon and Tiphys. In the quest for the fleece, she consults Athena, proposes that Cypris make Medea love Jason, hides Jason and his companions in mist on their approach to Aeetes’ palace, and drives Medea to flee. After Apsyrtus falls, she directs the voyage through storms, reversals, warnings, favorable winds, and protective mists, steering the Argonauts away from dangers. She commands Iris and calls on Thetis, whom she tended from infancy and married to Peleus, to help Argo pass Scylla, Charybdis, and the Wandering rocks. At the end, she sends nymphs to honor Jason and Medea’s marriage and inspires Arete’s judgment. Her power also extends to Macris, whom she drove from Euboea.

l: Argus, The Argonautica
s: Argus is a hero, shipwright, counselor, and helper of Athena and the Argonauts, described as son of Arestor and also as son of Phrixus. Under Athena’s guidance he helps build the swift Argo, then joins the assembled heroes despite Pelias’s wishes, wearing a bull hide and directing them to gird the ship with rope. After a shipwreck he seeks shelter, recounts the sons of Phrixus, and warns of Aeetes, the Colchians, and the sleepless serpent. His counsel guides Jason’s anchoring near the Phasis, is approved by Mopsus and the Argonauts, and ends with Jason sending him hastily to the city.

l: Athena, The Argonautica
s: Athena is a Tritonian goddess, daughter of Zeus and chief among goddesses, untouched by love’s darts. Bathed by Libyan warder nymphs at Trito’s waters, she fashions Argo with Argus, fitting into its stem a divine beam from Dodona’s oak. She promises courage to Jason, guides and propels the Argonauts through the Cyanean rocks, and has a shrine built by them in Crete. Later she plans with Hera to help the heroes seize the fleece and agrees to visit Cypris, though she knows no charms of desire.

l: Orpheus, The Argonautica
s: Orpheus is a singer, musician, seer, and son of Calliope, also called the son of Oeagrus. His lyre and songs have magical power, making music central to his role among Jason’s heroes aboard Argo. He carries Apollo’s sacred tripod, sings and plays at sacrifice, urges the Argonauts to honor Apollo of the Dawn, and leads their hymn. On the voyage, he ends Idas and Idmon’s quarrel by singing of creation and accompanies the rowing heroes. When the Sirens sing, his Bistonian lyre overcomes their voices and keeps the crew from landing. Near Atlas’s garden, he recognizes a divine portent and prays for water; the nymphs answer by bringing vegetation from the earth.

l: Thrace, The Argonautica
s: Thrace supplied the captive maids whom the Lemnian men brought back from their raids. After the conflict, the Lemnian men were said to live and plough fields in Thrace, and the Argonauts later sailed with Thracian land on one side. Winds from Thrace drive the Argo toward the Mount of Bears. The heroes later row to the Thracian harbour before climbing Dindymum.

l: Aeson, The Argonautica
s: Aeson, Jason’s father, lies in baleful old age, grieving and groaning over Jason’s departure.

l: Polyphemus, The Argonautica
s: Polyphemus, son of Eilatus, is a Lapith hero and former fighter against the Centaurs. Near Pegae, he hears Hylas’s cry, searches in fear of beasts or ambushers, meets Heracles, and reports Hylas’s disappearance; he is destined to found Cius among the Mysians.

l: Alcimede, The Argonautica
s: Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus and wife of Aeson, is an Achaean woman and Jason’s mother. Once admired, she grieves intensely as her only son departs under Pelias’s command, lamenting Phrixus’s flight.

l: Mopsus, The Argonautica
s: Mopsus, son of Ampycus, is a seer and prophet among the Argonauts, skilled at interpreting signs. He reads a halcyon’s cry as favorable, wakes Jason, and urges propitiation of the Mother of the gods to end a storm. He also interprets the dove and hawk, advising the Argonauts to call on Cytherea, seek the maiden, and follow Argus’s counsel. Despite his prophetic power, fate brings his death from a serpent’s bite; the Argonauts bury and honor him.

l: Libya, The Argonautica
s: At its furthest bounds, Libya is reached by Argonauts; it is a distant region they must toil through before Achaea. Its shore strands them without water, paths, or herdsmen, and they cross sandy wastes carrying Argo toward the Tritonian lake.

l: Apollo, The Argonautica
s: Apollo, also called Phoebus and Leto’s son, is a god associated with guidance, prophecy, protection, and powerful interventions. He promised Jason sea-paths and was invoked to guide Argo safely to Aeetes and back to Hellas. He granted Phineus prophecy, carried Cyrene from Haemonia to Libya, made her a long-lived huntress-nymph, and fathered Aristaeus, whom he sent to Ceos against pestilence. Later he appeared to the Argonauts and received sacrifice and song.

l: Telamon, The Argonautica
s: Telamon, son of Aeacus and comrade of Heracles, angrily accuses Jason of abandoning Heracles and nearly turns the heroes back; after Glaucus explains the divine purpose, he admits fault, seeks forgiveness, and reconciles with Jason.

l: Peleus, The Argonautica
s: Peleus, son of Aeacus, made his home in Phthia. He kills a white-tusked, murderous boar with a hunting spear after it wounds Idmon, then urges grieving heroes to continue their voyage. Husband of Thetis and father of Achilles, he receives her warning and recalls losing her by interrupting her attempt to make Achilles immortal.

l: Aegina, The Argonautica
s: is_a island [a beach where the Argonauts stopped] The Argonauts reach the beach of Aegina after leaving Anaphe. There they compete in an innocent race to fetch water and return it to the ship, a custom said to continue among the youths of the Myrmidons.

l: Tiphys, The Argonautica
s: Tiphys, son of Hagnias, is the skilled helmsman and pilot of Argo, urged to join by Athena and entrusted with the ship’s helm. He prepares and launches the vessel, wakes the heroes for departure, advises using a small anchorstone first, and commands its course. He guides the Argonauts safely through the Bosporus and Cyanean rocks amid huge waves, reassures Jason of Argo’s divine strength and easier labors ahead, and later dies of a short sickness far from his native land.

l: Heracles, The Argonautica
s: Heracles is a hero of mighty heart and strength, a son of Zeus, and is regarded as the bravest candidate for leadership. He is Hylas’s young companion’s protector: he has nurtured Hylas from childhood, while Hylas bears his arrows and guards his bow. When Jason summons the heroes, Heracles comes from Arcadia by way of Lyrceian Argos. He refuses leadership in Jason’s favor, shares Argo’s middle bench with Ancaeus, helps launch the ship, and uses his club in sacrifice. He presses the Argonauts to leave the Lemnian women and resume the fleece quest. In later fighting and travel, Heracles kills Earthborn attackers, Telecles, and Megabrontes, rows with exceptional force, and breaks an oar near the Mysian mainland. At Cius he enters the woods to cut a pine for a replacement oar. Learning from Polyphemus that Hylas is missing, he abandons the pine and searches frantically, threatening the Mysians with destruction unless Hylas’s fate is found. He is left behind there, against the Argonauts’ will; Lycus mourns the loss of his aid and recalls his defeat of Titias and subjugation of neighboring peoples. His destined course is to return to Argos, labor for Eurystheus, and afterward dwell with the immortals. His deeds include killing Theiodamas, driving birds from the Stymphalian lake with a bronze rattle, killing Ladon with hydra-gall arrows to take the golden apples, and making a spring near the Tritonian lake by striking rock with his foot. He acts against Eurystheus’s purpose and is the only hero able to withstand Aeetes’ spear.

l: Hylas, The Argonautica
s: Hylas, Theiodamas’s young, brave son and Heracles’s childhood-nurtured companion, bears Heracles’s arrows and guards his bow. Sent to Pegae for water and Heracles’s evening meal, he is seized by a water-nymph, who loves and marries him; the Mysians pledge to keep searching.

l: Idmon, The Argonautica
s: Idmon, Apollo’s prophet and a seer publicly counted as Abas’s son, reads sacrificial signs. He foretells the heroes’ return to Hellas with the fleece after countless trials, while knowing through augury that he will die on Asia’s mainland.

l: Polydeuces, The Argonautica
s: Polydeuces is a son of Leda, Tyndareus, and Zeus, skilled in guiding swift-footed steeds and boxing. As an Argonaut champion, he accepts Amycus’s challenge, withstands his attacks, and kills him with a blow above the ear. During fighting with the Bebrycians he kills Itymoneus and Mimas; the Mariandyni then welcome and worship him as a god, and song celebrates him.

l: Idas, The Argonautica
s: Idas, son of Aphareus and an Apharcian, wounds a white-tusked boar. Angrily rejecting aid from Cypris and omens from doves and hawks, he urges reliance on Enyalius, war, and mighty deeds.

l: Aeetes, The Argonautica
s: Aeetes is the powerful king and ruler of Colchis, the Colchians, Aea, and Cytaean Aea. He is a lord, father of Chalciope, Medea, Apsyrtus, and other offspring, and host to Phrixus. His palace holds the golden fleece, the object sought by Jason and his companions. He also possesses a prophecy received from Helios, dragon’s teeth given by the Tritonian goddess, a corslet from Ares, a golden helmet, and a chariot drawn by steeds gifted by Helios. As the heroes approach his land, Aeetes is expected to resist any effort to take the fleece. He receives Jason, the sons of Phrixus, Telamon, and Augeias, but becomes enraged when their purpose is known. He convenes the Colchians, denounces the Minyae, the sons of Phrixus, and the strangers, and invokes Helios’s warning of treachery by his offspring. He threatens punishment and calamity against the intruders and their allies. Aeetes promises the fleece if Jason fulfills a deadly contest, yet expects him to fail. He provides dragon’s teeth for the trial and watches it armed in his corslet, helmet, shield, and spear. Though he marvels at Jason’s strength, the destruction of the Earthborn men leaves him bitterly grieved. He returns to plan opposition and commands his captains to devise treachery against the heroes. After learning of Medea’s deeds, Aeetes plots against the heroes and pursues Medea and their ship with a large Colchian force, seeking to recover her and exact vengeance. He calls Helios and Zeus as witnesses to the theft and threatens his people unless they recover Medea. After Apsyrtus’s death, remaining Colchians fear his fierce anger and do not return home; his distant anger and authority are feared as a possible cause of war upon Hellas.

l: Colchis, The Argonautica
s: Colchis is the land of Aeetes and the Colchians, the destination of the heroes’ quest for the golden fleece. The Argonauts arrive there, encounter its people and customs, and become involved with Medea and Chalciope as help is discussed for the stranger. Medea then flees her home, and the heroes depart Colchis by water with the fleece while Aeetes and the Colchians pursue them.

l: Euphemus, The Argonautica
s: Euphemus, swift son of Poseidon who can run on the sea, carries and releases a trembling dove to test passage between the Cyanean rocks; when the rocks clip its tail-feathers, he urges the rowers to strain at their oars.

l: Hephaestus, The Argonautica
s: Hephaestus is a god associated with bronze anvils, fire, iron hammers, and smoke-grimed bellows. Through Cypris’s intervention he causes the Lemnian women’s alliance with the Argonauts, then stops his forge at Iris’s message and watches Argo pass.

l: Zetes, The Argonautica
s: Zetes, a winged son of Boreas, joins Calais in helping Phineus after securing an oath of safety, pursues the Harpies, and reports that Iris prevented their killing.

l: Calais, The Argonautica
s: Calais, a winged son of Boreas, joins Zetes in driving the Harpies from Phineus and pursues them nearly to the Floating Islands before Iris intervenes.

l: Minyae, The Argonautica
s: Minyae are the assembled heroes also called the Argonauts: nearby people use the name for the chiefs, many of whom claim descent from the daughters of Minyas. They travel aboard Argo in pursuit of the golden fleece in Colchis. At Lemnos they accept the Lemnian women’s invitation and hospitality, delay their departure, and leave after Heracles reproaches them. They meet and aid Phrixus’ shipwrecked sons, sacrifice with them, and sail to Aea and the Phasis. In Colchis, where they are strangers, Aeetes charges them with insolence and secret designs. During their escape, they make a covenant concerning Medea and the fleece, ambush and kill Apsyrtus, defeat the Colchian force, and continue with Medea’s assistance. Their return leads through islands, seas, Ister, Eridanus, Celtic waterways, the Stoechades, Aethalia and its Argoan harbour, and Aeaea, amid storms and other dangers. At Drepane they prepare to defend Medea against the Colchians, celebrate her marriage to Jason, receive gifts, and depart. Finally, stranded in Libya, they carry Argo across the desert, mourn Canthus and Mopsus, find Heracles’ spring, and resume sailing after Triton reveals the lake’s outlet.

l: Argonauts’ return voyage, The Argonautica
s: Argonauts’ return voyage is the perilous sea journey made by Jason and the heroes after escaping pursuit, carrying Jason from Aea toward Iolcus, Hellas, Achaea, and the land of Pelops with the golden fleece. Although the fleece quest began at Pelias’s command and was intended to prevent Jason’s return home, the return is sustained by the heroes’ hope, Jason’s prayer to Apollo, and Idmon’s prophecy that they will return with the fleece. The larger voyage includes delays at Lemnos, rites on Electra, crossings near Thrace and Imbros, and passage into the Hellespont after many shores. On the homeward course, after Apsyrtus falls, the heroes destroy the Colchian crew, row through sacred islands, receive aid from the Hylleans in exchange for Apollo’s tripod, and travel by the Colchian islands, Corcyra, Melite, Eridanus, and Rhodanus toward Ausonia. Hera’s intervention brings storm and reversal at Electra; dangerous waters, purification, and further delays follow before Aeaea. Finally, stranded in Syrtis and fearing return impossible, they regain hope when Libyan warder nymphs, Triton, and a lake outlet reveal a way back toward Achaea.

l: Pelias’s oracle, The Argonautica
s: foretells Pelias’s death [at the hands of the one-sandaled man] Pelias’s oracle foretells that a hateful doom will come upon him through the man he sees arriving with one sandal. Jason fulfills the sign after crossing the Anaurus and leaving one sandal in the flood.

l: Argonaut gathering, The Argonautica
s: is_a assembly of heroes [formed to join Jason] The gathering brings together numerous heroes from Thessaly, Greece, and other regions, including Orpheus, Heracles, Castor, Polydeuces, the sons of Aeacus, and many others. Athena urges Tiphys to join them, and Jason leads the assembled chiefs toward the voyage.

l: golden fleece quest, The Argonautica
s: The golden fleece quest is an expedition commanded by Pelias and undertaken by Jason, the Argonauts, and assembled heroes in the Argo toward Colchian land. Their journey includes deeds and wanderings, and they leave Lemnos after Heracles warns that remaining there will bring neither renown nor fleece. After mooring on the river Phasis, Jason and his companions pursue the fleece while Hera, Athena, Cypris, and Eros arrange aid. With Medea’s aid, the heroes obtain the fleece after Aeetes’ contests, then flee pursuing Colchians through a covenant, Apsyrtus’s deception, and violence.

l: Minyan heroes, The Argonautica
s: The Minyan heroes are a band of half-divine, exceptionally brave heroes, also called the Argonauts, who form the crew of the expedition to Colchis to obtain the golden fleece. They prepare and launch Argo from Pagasae, sacrifice to Apollo, choose Jason as leader, assign rowing places, and sail with Orpheus’s song. Their voyage brings both conflict and fellowship: they reach Lemnos, fight the Earthborn, mistakenly battle the Doliones, mourn Cyzicus with rites and games, and sacrifice on Dindymum. Hospitably received by the Mysians, they feast and take supplies, but depart without Heracles and Hylas; the resulting quarrel ends after Glaucus’s explanation and Jason’s reconciliation with Telamon. They support Polydeuces against the Bebrycians, rout them, care for the wounded, sacrifice, feast, and continue. At Colchis they cannot bend Jason’s spear, encourage him during his tasks, and rejoice in hope. They take Medea aboard, carry the golden fleece away, and prepare to defend their return. Their homeward journey is troubled: following Argus’s reading of Phineus’s prophecy, they sail toward Ister, become grief-stricken and fearful, pray after the ship’s warning, and are shaken by Hera’s cry.

l: Argonauts, The Argonautica
s: The Argonauts are a band of Hellenes, heroes, warriors, and Jason’s comrades: an Achaean expeditionary band that crews and sails on Argo in Jason’s quest for the Golden Fleece. Their voyage begins at Iolcos, from which they launch Argo for the land of Aeetes, passing Magnesia and Thrace before reaching Lemnos. Welcomed by Cyzicus and the Doliones, they defeat the Earthborn, but during a stormy nighttime return accidentally kill Cyzicus and other Doliones; after sacrifices to Rhea, they sail on. They aid the detained Phineus, receive his prophecy, and prepare for the Cyanean rocks on the way to Aea, at the edge of Pontus and the world. Given gifts by the Thynians, they sacrifice to the blessed twelve, carry a trembling dove aboard, pass the rocks, sacrifice to Apollo on Thynia, and swear an oath to help one another with concord of heart. Lycus welcomes them in the land of the Mariandyni and sends Dascylus with them. Near their goal, they wait unobserved in an ambush amid reed-beds. They decide Jason should first speak with Aeetes rather than use force; his challenge discourages them, though some volunteer and Argus proposes Medea’s help. They follow Mopsus’s interpretation of a divine sign, move Argo nearer shore, and depend on Medea for safety and return. Jason’s comrades greet him after his return to the ship, while Idas remains angry; Telamon and Aethalides seek the dragon’s teeth. On the homeward voyage, Thetis warns them. They evade the Sirens, pass the Wandering rocks with Nereids’ help, and go beyond Thrinacia. When wind fails they row night and day; Talos drives them from Crete until Medea devises a plan. After the Pall of Darkness and arrival at Anaphe, they race for water at Aegina and safely reach Pagasae.

l: Ancaeus, The Argonautica
s: Ancaeus, a son of Poseidon born to Astypalaea, dwells in Tegea and serves as the Argo’s helmsman. Sharing the middle bench with Heracles, he helps sacrifice a steer. Given courage by Hera, he urges the crew to continue and undertakes to guide the Argo.

l: Zeus, The Argonautica
s: Zeus is a god, king of gods, ruler of the Olympians, and ruler and observer of mortal affairs. He determines events by divine fate or counsel, including Heracles’ labors for Eurystheus and Polyphemus’s founding of Cius. He acts as messenger-sender, father of Athena, god of strangers and suppliants, god of wrath who aids slayers of men, and Zeus the Cleanser. He punishes Phineus with blindness and lingering old age for revealing divine will too fully, while granting the sons of Boreas tireless strength to pursue the Harpies. He is invoked in libations, receives altars and sacrifices, gives Sinope a home and grants her request for virginity, and is credited with rescuing Phrixus and his sons. He sends the north wind, storm, and shipwreck against the sons of Phrixus, then ends the rain at sunrise. Finally, angered by Apsyrtus’s killing, he decrees cleansing through Circe’s counsels and many woes before the perpetrators’ return.

l: Rhea, The Argonautica
s: is_identified_with Mother of the gods [the goddess invoked on Dindymum] Rhea is invoked as the venerable mother of Dindymum and the goddess dwelling in Phrygia. The heroes sacrifice to her with prayers, libations, armed dancing, and the clashing of shields, after which the winds cease and nature becomes abundant.

l: Phrixus, The Argonautica
s: Phrixus is an Aeolid, son of Athamas, who fled Hellas on a golden ram after escaping his stepmother’s wiles and a sacrifice prepared by his father. Zeus sent Hermes to guide him to a friendly host, and Aeetes received and honored him in Aea, valuing his exceptional gentleness and fear of the gods. At the Ram’s couch, by Hermes’ command, Phrixus sacrificed the golden wonder and established an altar to Zeus the Alder of Fugitives. Aeetes arranged his marriage to Chalciope, and they had sons. Phrixus grew old and died in Aeetes’ home, instructing his sons to seek Athamas’s possessions in Orchomenus. His escape, the intended sacrifice, and the golden fleece remain central to Jason’s voyage and Zeus’s wrath against the sons of Aeolus.

l: Apollo of the Dawn, The Argonautica
s: is_a epithet of Apollo [invoked as guide of embarkation] Apollo Embasius is honored with an altar on the shore before the ship departs. Jason prays to him to guide the ship and grant favorable winds, fulfilling the oracle that prompted the voyage.

l: the oracle of Apollo, The Argonautica
s: promises Jason [guidance on the sea voyage] The oracle of Apollo promised Jason that Apollo would show him the paths of the sea if he began the venture with sacrifice. Jason relies on this oracle when organizing the departure.

l: Idmon’s prophecy, The Argonautica
s: foretells Idmon’s death [somewhere on the mainland of Asia] Idmon’s prophecy declares that the heroes will return with the fleece but will face countless trials on the outward and homeward journeys. It also declares that Idmon will die somewhere on the mainland of Asia.

l: Argonauts’ voyage, The Argonautica
s: The Argonautic expedition is the voyage undertaken by the Argonauts to obtain the golden fleece, intended to atone for the intended sacrifice of Phrixus and guided by the Cyprian goddess toward a glorious outcome. It begins when Jason and the heroes leave Pagasae after preparing and launching Argo and sacrificing to Apollo, then sail toward Lemnos. Phineus foretells their route through the Cyanean rocks and Pontus to Aea and warns them to obey divine signs. After Idmon and Tiphys die, they continue past rivers, headlands, islands, and many peoples, reach the island of Ares using a shield-and-noise defense, and later enter the Phasis near Aeetes. As they approach Aeetes, Medea fears great evil but agrees to help the stranger complete the contest.

l: the sacrifice to Apollo, The Argonautica
s: is_offered_at the altar to Apollo [before embarkation] Jason and the heroes build an altar to Apollo Actius and Embasius on the shore and sacrifice two steers. They burn the thigh bones in fat, pour libations, and pray for safe travel and a favorable wind.

l: Iolcus, The Argonautica
s: Iolcus is a city and the heroes’ homeland, Jason’s home in Haemonia and a royal center. The voyage begins there, with the ship leaving nearby Pagasae. Jason is expected to return to Iolcus with the golden fleece, aided by Medea; she asks to come there, and he promises her honor in Hellas and a shared bridal chamber.

l: Pagasae, The Argonautica
s: Pagasae is a beach and harbour where Argo lies and the heroes assemble. The Argonauts come ashore, ready the ship, sacrifice to Apollo, and sail away. After leaving Aegina, they return peacefully to its beach, with no further adventure or opposing tempest.

l: Hellas, The Argonautica
s: Hellas is a land, Jason’s homeland, and the home and origin of the Argonauts. The voyage begins from Hellas, with Jason and the heroes sailing to Aeetes’ land after the golden fleece, as Phrixus had earlier traveled from Hellas to Aea. Hellas matters as the hoped-for end of the quest: the heroes seek safe return there, and the fleece is to be borne back to it. Jason’s success or failure brings shame or renown to all Hellas; he promises Aeetes that its people will proclaim the king’s fame and promises Medea honor among its women and men. By the venture’s end, Jason intends to return with both the fleece and Medea as his wedded wife.

l: Mount Pelion, The Argonautica
s: overlooks the sea [its nymphs watch the launch] Mount Pelion overlooks the departure route, and its nymphs watch the heroes wielding the oars. The Argonauts pass its rugged sides and the Sepian headland before continuing onward.

l: Lemnos, The Argonautica
s: Lemnos, the Sintian isle in the Aegean Sea, is a fertile island whose men were massacred by its women. Reached by the heroes after the wind fails, it receives the Minyae; Hypsipyle offers Jason sovereignty, and the Argonauts later depart, with an alliance intended to reinhabit it.

l: Olympus, The Argonautica
s: contains the palace of Zeus [the palace is in its orchard] Olympus contains Cypris's palace and the orchard of Zeus, where Cypris finds Eros. Eros then passes through Olympus's high gates and travels downward toward the earth.

l: golden ram, The Argonautica
s: A ram made entirely of gold by Hermes carries Phrixus from Hellas to Aea, where Phrixus sacrifices it to Zeus and its fleece remains.

l: the Argonauts’ departure from Iolcos, The Argonautica
s: is_accompanied_by the women of Iolcos [lamentation and prayers for a safe return] The Argonauts’ departure from Iolcos is prepared through Jason’s leadership, the launching of Argo at Pagasae, and the sacrifice to Apollo. They finally leave the harbour by rowing and sailing along the coast.

l: the launch of Argo, The Argonautica
s: occurs_at the beach of Pagasae [after the ship is dragged into the sea] The heroes dig a trench, place rollers beneath Argo, and push the ship into the sea using their strength and reversed oars. They then install the mast, sails, stores, and rowing benches before setting out.

l: Lemnian men, The Argonautica
s: The Lemnian men reject lawful wives for Thracian captive maids; Lemnian women slay them in the massacre, while surviving men are said to dwell on snowy Thracian tilths.

l: Lemnian women, The Argonautica
s: The Lemnian women, responsible for the Lemnian massacre after a marriage-bed conflict, killed their men, including husbands and captive maids’ partners. They took up cattle-tending, agriculture, armour, and warfare, feared the Thracians, assembled under Hypsipyle, welcomed and allied with the Argonauts, then lamented their departure.

l: Hypsipyle, The Argonautica
s: Hypsipyle, Thoas’s daughter, spares him during the Lemnian massacre and sends him away hidden in a chest, then becomes queen of Lemnos. She leads the women’s assembly, proposes gifts for the Minyae, welcomes Jason, conceals the killings, and tearfully offers him Lemnos and Thoas’s sceptre.

l: Thoas, The Argonautica
s: Thoas, king of the Lemnian people before the massacre and father of Hypsipyle, is spared by her, escapes in a hollow chest to Oenoe, and fathers Sicinus with Oenoe.

l: Cypris, The Argonautica
s: Cypris is a goddess, wife of Hephaestus and mother of Eros, with a palace built by Hephaestus and rule over Eryx. She brings wrath, infatuation, and desire: she punishes Lemnian men, then restores Lemnos through the women’s desire, and is propitiated by them. She also saves Butes, makes a water-nymph love Hylas, and sends Eros to make Aeetes’ daughter love Jason.

l: Aphrodite, The Argonautica
s: Aphrodite is a goddess, also called Cyprian goddess, Cytherea, and Cypris; her gentle bird is the dove, and Mopsus calls on her to aid the Argonauts.

l: Ares, The Argonautica
